questions.q: State the definition of a rectangle in one sentence using the words "quadrilateral", "right angles", and "parallelogram".
questions.a: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles, or equivalently a parallelogram with one right angle. A wrong answer that only says "four equal angles" misses the 90° requirement; a student who says "a parallelogram with equal sides" is confusing rectangle with rhombus/square.

questions.q: In a rectangle ABCD, side AB = 8 cm and side BC = 5 cm. Without measuring, what are the lengths of CD and AD? Explain why you are certain.
questions.a: CD = 8 cm and AD = 5 cm because opposite sides of a rectangle (being a parallelogram) are equal. A wrong answer that gives CD = 5 cm and AD = 8 cm shows the student does not understand which sides are opposite; an answer of "cannot be determined" reveals the student does not connect rectangle to parallelogram properties.

questions.q: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS intersecting at O. If PR = 10 cm, what is the length of QS? What is the length of PO?
questions.a: QS = 10 cm (diagonals of a rectangle are equal). PO = 5 cm (diagonals bisect each other, so PO = half of PR). A wrong answer of QS = 5 cm or PO = 10 cm indicates confusion between "equal diagonals" and "bisecting diagonals"; a student who says PO = 2.5 cm might be halving the wrong segment.

questions.q: A carpenter builds a frame with opposite sides equal: 120 cm and 80 cm. He measures one angle and finds it is 85°. Is this frame a rectangle? Justify your answer using the definition.
questions.a: No, it is not a rectangle. Although opposite sides are equal (making it a parallelogram), a rectangle requires all angles to be 90° (or at least one angle 90°). An 85° angle violates the definition. A student who says "yes, because opposite sides are equal" is confusing parallelogram with rectangle; a student who says "no, because adjacent sides are not equal" is confusing rectangle with square.

questions.q: Rohan claims: "Every rectangle is a parallelogram, but not every parallelogram is a rectangle." Evaluate this statement and give a counterexample for the second part.
questions.a: The statement is correct. A rectangle satisfies the parallelogram condition (opposite sides parallel and equal) and adds the right-angle condition. A counterexample for "not every parallelogram is a rectangle" is a rhombus with angles 60° and 120° (or any parallelogram without right angles). A wrong evaluation that says "false, all parallelograms are rectangles" shows a fundamental misunderstanding of the hierarchy; a student who gives a square as a counterexample doesn't realize a square IS a rectangle.

questions.q: Create a real-life problem (using Indian context: rupees, metres, etc.) that requires using the property "opposite sides of a rectangle are equal" to find an unknown length. Write the problem and its solution.
questions.a: Example problem: "A rectangular plot has a perimeter of 140 m. Its length is 10 m more than its breadth. Find the length and breadth." Solution uses opposite sides equal to set up 2(l+b)=140 and l=b+10. A poor answer gives a problem that doesn't need the property (e.g., direct area calculation) or a solution that doesn't explicitly use "opposite sides equal", showing the student cannot design a task targeting this specific property.
